vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is a forty-five-year-old chef who carries himself with the careful precision of someone accustomed to controlling his environment. He moves through the world with measured deliberation-the same focused intensity he brings to his kitchen, where he has spent the last twenty years building a reputation for exquisite contemporary Pacific cuisine. When he speaks, his voice is measured and quiet, as though he is rationing his words.

Seven years ago, Marcus experienced a sexual assault by a colleague during a late-night service at a restaurant where he was working as a sous chef. The assault occurred in the walk-in freezer after closing, and the memory of it-the cold, the darkness, the violation-remains vivid and intrusive. Marcus doesn't discuss it directly; instead, he describes how his body still reacts to cold temperatures, how his breathing becomes shallow when doors close behind him, how the smell of certain prep ingredients can transport him back to that moment with startling intensity.

In the years since, Marcus has developed an intricate system of avoidance. He no longer works with the freezer himself; he has trained his staff extensively to manage it, though he recognizes this is unusual and sometimes catches himself explaining it away to new employees. He prefers to work during early service when the kitchen is busier and more populated. The irony is not lost on him-he chose cooking because it was his sanctuary, a place where he could create beauty and control outcomes. Now his sanctuary contains landmines.

His divorce, finalized three years ago, was partly precipitated by his inability to be intimate with his then-wife. Marcus describes this period with shame and resignation, as though it were simply the natural consequence of what happened to him. He doesn't articulate anger at his ex-wife; instead, he seems to have internalized the failure as his own moral failing, another way the assault continues to dictate the shape of his life.

Marcus sleeps poorly. He goes to bed late, often after midnight, and wakes between three and four in the morning with his heart racing. He describes these early mornings as the worst part of his day-the hours before dawn when his apartment is quiet and his mind becomes loud. He has tried sleeping medication but found the grogginess incompatible with the precision his work demands. So he tolerates the insomnia, using the quiet hours to prep ingredients or simply to wait for daylight.

He experiences persistent hypervigilance in public spaces. In restaurants where he dines, he positions himself with a clear view of exits and entrances. In crowds, he feels exposed and vulnerable despite his physical size. He startles easily when touched unexpectedly, even in benign contexts. A hand on his shoulder from a staff member can send his nervous system into overdrive.

What strikes most is Marcus's careful compartmentalization. At work, he is composed, professional, commanding respect through his culinary expertise and his steady presence. His staff admires him, though some have noted he maintains emotional distance. Away from the kitchen, he is increasingly isolated. He has declined social invitations, avoided relationships, and withdrawn from the close friendships he once maintained. He tells himself this is simply who he is now-someone whose capacity for connection was fundamentally altered by what happened.

Marcus came to therapy because a trusted mentor finally insisted. He doesn't hold much hope that talking about it will change anything. He has learned to live around the trauma, building his life in the spaces it doesn't occupy. But those spaces are shrinking.
